definition: Quadratic programming (QP) is the process of solving certain mathematical optimization problems involving quadratic functions.
details: Specifically, one seeks to optimize (minimize or maximize) a multivariate quadratic function subject to linear constraints on the variables. Quadratic programming is a type of nonlinear programming. "Programming" in this context refers to a formal procedure for solving mathematical problems. This usage dates to the 1940s and is not specifically tied to the more recent notion of "computer programming." To avoid confusion, some practitioners prefer the term "optimization" — e.g., "quadratic optimization."

explainer.lead: Quadratic programming (QP) solves optimization problems with a quadratic objective and linear constraints, a workhorse for problems where cost grows nonlinearly with the variables. It matters because many practical engineering and learning problems fit this shape exactly.

tiers.eli5: You're trying to find the lowest point of a bowl-shaped surface, but you can only move along straight-line fences — QP finds the best spot you're allowed to reach.
tiers.practitioner: Engineers use QP solvers inside model-predictive control, portfolio optimization, and SVM training. A common pitfall is assuming convexity: with an indefinite quadratic term the problem can have multiple local optima and the solver may return one of them.
tiers.paperLevel: Minimize (1/2) x^T Q x + c^T x subject to A x <= b, where Q is symmetric; if Q is positive semidefinite the problem is convex and solvable in polynomial time, otherwise it is generally hard.

explainer.example: Allocating weights across assets to minimize portfolio variance subject to a budget constraint and per-asset caps is a standard QP.
